The photos in the living room
It is Nora’s first morning in Cluj. Mrs Pop invites her for a coffee in the living room. On one wall there are lots of old and new photos.
Good morning, Mrs Pop! What a lot of photos you have!
Good morning, Nora! Yes, I have a big family. Look, this is my husband, Vasile.
He’s very elegant! Where is he now?
He is no longer alive. But I have two children: a son and a daughter.
And are they here, in Cluj?
My daughter, Ioana, is in Cluj. She’s a doctor. My son, Andrei, is an engineer in Timișoara.
And the boy with the violin? Who is he?
Ah, that’s Radu, my grandson, Ioana’s son. He’s twenty-nine. And you, dear? Do you have brothers or sisters?
I have a sister. She’s twenty-five and a student in Stockholm.
And how old are you, if it’s not a secret?
It’s not a secret! I’m thirty-two. I have no husband and no children. I only have a cat, at my parents’.
A cat! Then Mițu has a girlfriend in Sweden!

In Romanian the stress is not written, but it matters. It usually falls on the second-to-last syllable: “familie” is stressed on “mi”, “bunică” on “ni”. Listen to and repeat every new word.
“ie” and “ia” are read with a short gliding “i”: “familie” = “fa-mi-li-e”, but “fiică” = “fi-i-că”. At the beginning of a word, the “e” in “este”, “el”, “ea” is read “ye”: “este” = “yeste”.
A short “i” at the end of a word is barely heard: “ani” sounds almost like “an”, and “frați” almost like “fraț”. But “copii” (plural) has two “i”s and both are heard.
Many feminine words end in “ă”. Say it clearly but briefly: “mamă”, “soră”, “bunică”.
2nd person plural; also the polite form
Negation works as with “a fi”, with “nu” in front: “nu am”, “nu ai”, “nu are”. In speech, “nu am” is often shortened to “n-am”.
I don’t have time. (= Nu am timp.)
In Romanian, age is expressed with the verb “a avea” (to have), as in French, Spanish or Italian: “Am 32 de ani.” (I am 32.)
From 20 upwards, “de” appears before the noun: “opt ani”, but “douăzeci de ani”, “treizeci și doi de ani”. You will learn the full rule in chapter 4.
Romanian has three genders. The neuter is special: in the singular it behaves like a masculine, and in the plural like a feminine.
usually male people and animals; ends in a consonant, -u or -e
many objects; “un” in the singular, “două” in the plural
A trick: say “un … / două …”. If it works, the noun is neuter: “un oraș / două orașe”, “un proiect / două proiecte”.
4. The indefinite article: un, o, niște
“Niște” means “some, a few, an unspecified amount”. It can often be left out: “Am frați” or “Am niște frați”.
Don’t confuse “o” (the feminine article: “o soră”) with the pronoun “o” (“o văd” = I see her). The context helps.
Only “unu” and “doi” change with gender. With neuter nouns in the plural you use the feminine form: “două orașe”.
When you count on its own (1, 2, 3…), you say “unu, doi, trei”. Before a noun you say “un frate”, “o soră”.

The possessive usually comes AFTER the noun, and the noun takes the definite article (-ul, -a): “soțul meu” (my husband), “fiica mea” (my daughter). There is more about the definite article in chapter 3.
A common exception: “mama”, “tata” are used with both the article and the possessive: “mama mea” (my mother), “tatăl meu” (my father). Without the article you don’t say “mamă mea”.
